verdicts.trueWording: Conceptual metaphors play an important role in the work
verdicts.note: Crossref JATS abstract for the Kuts/Uholkova article (Intelligence. Personality. Civilization 2(21) 2020, 27-37) carries the sentence word for word; the surrounding sentences fix the novel as The Left Hand of Darkness and repeat that the metaphors matter.

verdicts.trueWording: does not set goals to show the image of darkness as negative
verdicts.note: Same Crossref abstract, sentence on the distinction of the author's style; the subject is 'the author', i.e. Le Guin, named in the preceding sentences.

verdicts.trueWording: Always Coming Home: “Ethnography, unBible, and Utopian Satire”
verdicts.note: paradoxa.com volume-21 page shows the title, 'Edited by Sylvia Kelso', and the Erlich item at pages 137-166, verbatim. No year appears anywhere on the page (grep for 2009 over the raw HTML returns zero hits; the only years present are 1995/2000/2015/2019/2020/2024/2025), so the date limb is unsupported by this source.

Strange Horizons, Mazin Saleem, 26 November 2018, section 'There and back again'. The note glosses the Pig People, whom the same sentence calls a neighbouring tribe. The page's own wording is 'a note' rather than 'an editorial note'; it is set apart from the story and from a named commentator, so the editorial-apparatus reading holds.

verdicts.trueWording: purposefully left the accents off Kesh names until the Back
verdicts.note: Same Strange Horizons article, late section on language: introduced by 'she explained that', so it is Le Guin's explanation as Saleem reports it, and it continues 'of the Book'.

verdicts.trueWording: Tolkien's world has almost no ethnographic detail
verdicts.note: dannyreviews.com, Danny Yee, dated August 1995, opening paragraph; the same sentence completes the contrast with Le Guin's world having no history.

verdicts.trueWording: it is a fictional ethnography rather than a novel
verdicts.note: Same opening paragraph; the subject is Always Coming Home, compared with the Silmarillion rather than The Lord of the Rings.

verdicts.trueWording: she ended up writing five short stories plus a descriptive essay
verdicts.note: troypress.com 'A History of Earthsea' (11 Nov 2023) carries the quoted clause verbatim in the world-building paragraph, but the string 'Description of Earthsea' never occurs on the page (zero hits over the raw HTML) and the five stories are not tied to Tales from Earthsea in that sentence.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the identification of that essay as 'A Description of Earthsea'

verdicts.trueWording: research into nonexistent history is to tell the story
verdicts.note: Same troypress.com paragraph, introduced by 'She wrote', and the sentence ends with finding out what happened. The page does not itself name the Tales from Earthsea foreword as the origin, but the claim sentence does not assert that.

verdicts.trueWording: the 8.4 month gestation period and the 6 to 8 month
verdicts.note: vector-bsfa.com, reviewed by Nick Hubble, review first appeared in The BSFA Review. The block quote is cited '(91)' and the next line identifies it as the field notes of Ong Tot Oppong, chapter 'The Question of Sex'. Both figures sit in one sentence, the decimal then the range.

verdicts.trueWording: a reference narrative covering Earthsea's peoples, languages, history, and magic
verdicts.note: en.wikipedia.org Tales from Earthsea, contents sentence: the book ends with 'A Description of Earthsea', so described.

verdicts.trueWording: almost thirty pages of Earthsea lore
verdicts.note: openlibrary.org search-inside results page fetched raw; the first snippet is from 'Ursula K. Le Guin beyond genre: fiction for children and adults' by Michael Cadden and reads that the book concludes with 'A Description of Earthsea', so many pages of lore.

verdicts.trueWording: a text that is neither story nor afterword
verdicts.note: Second search-inside snippet from the same Cadden volume on the same raw results page: Tales from Earthsea ends with 'A Description of Earthsea', so classed.

verdicts.trueWording: with a scholar's seriousness and eye for detail
verdicts.note: bookreporter.com review of Tales from Earthsea, reviewed by Kathy Weissman; the sentence says Le Guin has constructed her alternate world in those terms and cites the appendix 'A Description of Earthsea'.

verdicts.trueWording: who are to reports as squirrels are to nuts
verdicts.note: ursulakleguin.com Foreword: The Birthday of the World, paragraph on 'The Matter of Seggri'; the antecedent on the page is the Historians of Hain and their archives.
